title: More records, beyond Victor
items: About 50 new records from Wikimedia Commons, all public domain and made between 1902 and 1924: Edison, Columbia, Gramophone, Brunswick and other labels, not just Victor.

New voices and players include Feodor Chaliapin, Adelina Patti, Alessandro Moreschi (the last castrato), Rosa Ponselle, Leo Slezak, Lucrezia Bori, Claire Dux and Antonio Paoli, plus Edvard Grieg playing his own Wedding Day at Troldhaugen, Rachmaninoff's C-sharp minor Prelude, and Gustav Holst conducting The Planets.
The Library has them too, with links to each file on Wikimedia Commons.

title: More scores, an exact year, music-only clues and a library
items: Score tab: no more audio, just more of the score after each miss. Far more music: 108 composers instead of 3, including Beethoven sonatas and string quartets, Bach, Corelli, Debussy, Grieg, Liszt, Schumann, Schubert, Brahms, Tchaikovsky, Dvořák, Bartók, over a thousand art songs and many string quartets. Score clues are music facts too: the poet, the year written, the key.
The year: keep guessing until you hit the exact year. A close guess still earns points (half a point less for each year off), and there's no more "earlier" or "later" hint.

Clues are all about music now: teachers, pupils, conservatories, where people lived and worked, premieres, librettists, and what else happened in music that year. Gone: burial places, family, letter counts and how many recordings someone has in the game.
New Library tab: every recording in the game, searchable by composer, performer, piece or year, with downloads (MP3, WAV, MIDI or the Library of Congress audio).
Songs in the Score tab keep their lyrics.

Relationships that matter in music are back as clues, for example Liszt's daughter Cosima, who married Wagner and von Bülow. Only relatives and partners who worked in music, or married a composer, are mentioned.

title: Score mode, a better piano, downloads and real clues
items: New Score tab: name the piece from a few bars of sheet music. Each miss shows more bars and a clue, and you can listen to the bars. Chopin (his first editions), plus Mozart and Haydn sonatas.
A much better piano: seven loudness layers instead of one, the soft thump of keys and dampers, pedal noise and a little room sound.
Download the whole recording after a round: rolls as MP3, lossless WAV or the original MIDI; records as the Library of Congress MP3.
Leaving the tab no longer stops the music, and the clip still ends exactly where it should.
Clues now work like quiz bowl: they start with specific, little-known facts (a teacher, a burial place, a librettist, what else happened that year) and get more obvious.
No more useless clues: rolls don't tell you it's piano music, and once you know the composer you get no more composer clues.
Pieces in a published set (Chopin's Études, Op. 10; Brahms's Intermezzi, Op. 117): name the set first, then pick which piece from a second list. The right set alone is worth 2 points.
Fixed duplicates: Madam/Madama Butterfly, Loreley/LORELEI, Stephanie gavotte/gavota, and a Schubert impromptu listed twice.

title: Pick your hints
items: Each miss still earns one hint, but now you choose what it's about: the performer, the piece or the year.
Each kind goes from vague to specific. Performer hints include who they were (for example "an Irish tenor"), when they lived, how many recordings they're on, and their initials.
Piece hints include the kind of music, who the composer was, the composer's name, and the kind of piece or key.
Year hints include the decade, how old the composer and performer were, and a 5-year window.
The 1 point for naming only the composer goes away once you open the hint that names the composer.

The year is now guessed together with the performers and the piece. Each guess can include a year; within 2 years counts, and a wrong year tells you whether to go earlier or later. Sooner is worth more: 2 points on the first two tries, then 1.5, then 1.
Naming the right composer no longer earns a point or saves a try once the composer hint has been shown.
Audio now stops when you switch to another tab, instead of playing on.
Dropped the piano-roll brand name from the player and the hints. The first hint now gives the composer's dates instead.
Added this changelog.

title: Cleanup
items: Performers listed under two names are merged, such as Eugenie Adam and Eugenie Adam-Benard.
Fame ratings fixed: studio orchestras no longer count as famous.
A set of pieces no longer appears beside its own numbered pieces. For example, Chopin's Op. 28 now lists Preludes Nos. 1–24, and a roll of several preludes accepts any of them.
Titles in other languages and other spellings of the same work count as one answer, such as Arabeske and Arabesque.
Composers use their usual short names, such as Beethoven rather than van Beethoven.
Popular songs, dance music and instrumental solos were removed. Lieder and other classical art songs have their own genre.

title: Opera, orchestral music and practice
items: Added about 900 opera, orchestral and art song records from the Library of Congress, alongside the piano rolls.
New Practice tab with filters for format, genre, recording years and how famous the composer and performer are.
Each puzzle plays a random part of the piece, and only misses lengthen the clip.
The piece box searches about 8,800 works as you type.
The roll display never shows notes past the part you've unlocked.

title: Launch
items: Whose Hands launched with 450 piano rolls recorded between 1905 and 1925.
